title: Viramontes v. Cook County
backgroundAndFacts:
Cook County, Illinois enacted the Firearms Assault Weapons Ban, which prohibits the possession, sale, and transfer of semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns that meet certain criteria—commonly called 'assault weapons'—as well as magazines capable of holding more than ten rounds of ammunition. Cutberto Viramontes and other plaintiffs, who are law-abiding residents of Cook County, challenged the ordinance as an unconstitutional violation of their Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms. The federal district court upheld the ban, and the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed that decision in June 2025.

The Seventh Circuit's ruling came after the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, which established that gun regulations must be grounded in the historical tradition of firearm regulation in America at the time of the Founding. The Seventh Circuit concluded that the banned firearms are not protected by the Second Amendment because they are 'like' weapons used by the military and thus fall outside ordinary civilian use. Petitioners argued that this reasoning contradicts Bruen and the Court's earlier ruling in District of Columbia v. Heller, which held that Americans have a right to possess arms 'in common use' for self-defense.

The Supreme Court consolidated this case with a related Connecticut case (No. 25-566) challenging that state's similar assault weapons ban. Together, these cases present the Court with a direct opportunity to resolve a significant split among the lower courts over whether bans on commonly owned semiautomatic firearms are constitutionally permissible.
legalQuestion: Whether Cook County's ban on semiautomatic firearms and certain magazines violates the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms as interpreted by the Supreme Court's historical-tradition test.
significance:
This case is one of the most consequential Second Amendment cases the Supreme Court has taken up in years, directly testing the reach of its 2022 Bruen decision. Dozens of states and localities have enacted laws banning so-called assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, and lower courts have reached conflicting conclusions about whether those laws survive constitutional scrutiny. A ruling here will likely determine the fate of similar bans in states such as California, Maryland, and New York.

The case also forces the Court to clarify what types of firearms are protected under the Second Amendment—specifically whether semiautomatic rifles like the AR-15, which are among the most commonly owned firearms in the United States, fall within the scope of the right established in Heller and Bruen. The outcome will have immediate, practical consequences for millions of gun owners and for state and local governments seeking to regulate firearms for public safety purposes.

parties.coreArgument: Cook County's ban on semiautomatic firearms and standard-capacity magazines violates the Second Amendment because these weapons are in common use by law-abiding Americans for self-defense and other lawful purposes, and no historical tradition from the Founding era supports an outright ban on such commonly owned arms. The Seventh Circuit wrongly created a 'military-style' exception to Second Amendment protection that finds no support in Heller, McDonald, or Bruen.
supportingPoints: Semiautomatic firearms are owned by tens of millions of Americans and are among the most popular firearms in the country, placing them squarely within the 'common use' protection recognized in Heller.

The Seventh Circuit's test—which excludes arms 'like' military weapons—contradicts Heller, which recognized that the Second Amendment protects weapons with militia or military utility that are also suitable for civilian use.

Under Bruen's historical-tradition test, the government cannot point to any analogous Founding-era law banning an entire category of commonly owned arms, making the Cook County ordinance unconstitutional.
Banning the most effective tools available for home self-defense undermines the core purpose of the Second Amendment as articulated by the Supreme Court.

parties.coreArgument: Cook County's Firearms Assault Weapons Ban is a constitutionally permissible regulation because the banned weapons are unusually dangerous, military-style arms that fall outside the Second Amendment's protections, which were never intended to guarantee civilian access to battlefield weapons. The ordinance is consistent with a deep historical tradition of legislatures regulating especially dangerous weapons to protect public safety.
supportingPoints: Semiautomatic assault weapons are not protected by the Second Amendment because they are uniquely dangerous weapons designed for military combat, not ordinary self-defense, and thus fall outside the historical scope of civilian arms.

Even if the Second Amendment applies, there is a sufficient historical tradition of governments restricting access to particularly dangerous and unusual weapons, which supports the County's regulation.

The Heller decision itself recognized that certain weapons, particularly those most useful in military service, are not protected for civilian ownership, and Congress and state legislatures have long regulated such arms.
Public safety interests and the devastating harm caused by mass shootings involving these weapons justify the County's legislative judgment, which courts should respect.

citedPrecedents.caseName: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Bruen established the current constitutional test for evaluating gun regulations, requiring that any firearms restriction be rooted in the historical tradition of regulation at the time of the Founding; both parties invoke it as the controlling framework.

Heller established the individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense and held that arms 'in common use' are constitutionally protected, while suggesting that unusually dangerous or military-only weapons may be regulated; both sides claim its support.
McDonald incorporated the Second Amendment against state and local governments through the Fourteenth Amendment, making it applicable to Cook County's ordinance.

Miller has been cited by respondents for the proposition that weapons with a military character not suitable for ordinary civilian use may be regulated, though petitioners argue Heller reinterpreted Miller's meaning.

Petitioners cite Caetano for the principle that the Second Amendment protects modern weapons not in existence at the Founding, and that courts cannot limit protection only to weapons available in 1791.

This Seventh Circuit decision, which upheld assault weapons bans in Illinois municipalities and was the precursor to the ruling in this case, is central to the legal framework being challenged by petitioners.
